views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep negotiating through the Liu He–Lighthizer/Mnuchin channel and treat the March 1 List-3 hike as the immediate problem to defuse, not a cue to retaliate again. Put concrete purchase volumes (soy, energy, aircraft) on the table as the price of a deadline slide or a standstill at 10%, while refusing a U.S.-run enforcement mechanism that would police industrial policy inside China. Do not add tariffs or further hostage-taking now; do not pre-commit structural rollback of Made in China 2025 or a full tariff climb-down before Washington offers a matching tariff freeze.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high but not existential. The United States already covers ~$250B of Chinese goods (25% on the $50B Lists 1–2; 10% on List 3), and the G20 truce only paused the scheduled jump of List 3 to 25% on ~$200B (timeline 2018-09-24, 2018-12-01). That hike, if triggered, would hit the same export machine already showing stress: 2018 GDP slowed to 6.6% (three-decade low), Q4 to 6.4%, official manufacturing PMI was still in contraction at 49.5 in January, and December exports fell 4.4%. Firm-level tech targeting is live and distinct from tariffs: the ZTE denial order (2018-04-16), Meng’s arrest the same day as the G20 dinner, and the 2019-01-28 unsealing of Huawei/Meng fraud and sanctions charges plus a formal extradition request. That combination sits near the CHN +0.5 anchor (export sectors + national-champion targeting) but is pulled back from +0.5–+1.0 by mixed near-term data and an open diplomatic window: January dollar exports rose 9.1% (Lunar New Year caveats apply), China–US goods imports into the United States have already collapsed (IMPCH from ~$52.1B in Oct-2018 to ~$33.0B in Feb-2019), and Trump has publicly said March 1 is “not a magical date” and that the deadline could “slide” if a real deal is close. Action should therefore stay on the negotiate band, not escalate. Escalation would make the 25% hike more likely and deepen the export/employment hit China is already trying to offset with stimulus. Full concession or concede_purchases as the headline move is premature: talks have produced purchase progress but no matching U.S. offer to roll back existing 301 tariffs, and Lighthizer is still demanding “enforcement, enforcement, enforcement” plus structural IP/subsidy changes China has not accepted (timeline 2019-01-30, 2019-02-14). Purchases can be used inside the negotiation to buy time and split Trump (who wants a “big deal” and farm-belt wins) from Lighthizer (who rejects a purchases-only outcome). Hold the Meng/Huawei file on a separate legal-political track rather than trading core industrial policy for her release; Trump has already floated politicizing the case, which is leverage, not a reason to fold on sovereignty.
key_factors: Pending March 1 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% on ~$200B still the binding near-term shock
Existing $250B Section 301 coverage plus Huawei/Meng indictment is the core threat to exports and tech champions
Domestic slowdown is real (2018 GDP 6.6%, PMI <50) but January trade was not a collapse
Talks are live with reported purchase progress and an unresolved enforcement/sovereignty gap
Trump has softened the hard deadline, creating room to negotiate a standstill without new Chinese escalation
No matching U.S. tariff rollback is on the table, so purchases should be bargaining chips inside talks, not a unilateral concession

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
G20: 90-day negotiation window; planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended. Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
US DOJ unseals fraud and sanctions-related charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests Meng's extradition from Canada.
Lighthizer and Mnuchin in Beijing. Purchase commitments discussed; enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer issues unresolved.
Another round of talks (through Feb 15). Progress reported on purchases; enforcement mechanism still disputed.
US imports from China fell from $52.08B (2018-10) to $33.03B (2019-02), a ~34% decline over the window.
China's 2018 growth slowed to 6.6%, lowest since 1990; Q4 growth 6.4%. NBS cited downward pressure; trade dispute proving costly.
Official manufacturing PMI 49.5 in January (still below 50), after 49.4 in December.
Trump said March 1 'is not a magical date'; talks continue in Washington after Beijing round did not yield a deal.
Trump said he could let the March 1 deadline 'slide for a little while' if close to a real deal, but is 'not inclined' to.
January dollar exports +9.1% y/y (vs forecast -3.2%); imports from the US -41.2% y/y. Lunar New Year timing caveat.
Lighthizer: 'If we can get an agreement, it's worth nothing without enforcement.' SCMP: 'enforcement, enforcement, enforcement.'
